technology.name: FlexiBUS peripheral standard
technology.description: Shared peripheral transport, discovery and device-class contracts; pointing devices are a later optional class, not another core standard.

specification.description: FlexiBUS v1 defines the peripheral transport used at the Aurelia launch on 5 June 1978. The January 1975 agreement is a development commitment, not proof of release. Independent compatibility programmes are explicitly published on 5 May 1979; wider publication and new host implementations do not establish a new transport version. The pointing-device class is introduced with the NCC presentation on 7 June 1982 and uses the existing transport. It is not part of the 1978 baseline and does not imply unrestricted hot-plugging. Transport requirements, class extensions and measured implementation qualification remain distinct. TUI owns user-facing keyboard and pointer meanings.

specification.description:
1978 baseline and later published compatibility programme. Requirements and qualification gates are not assertions of completed tests.

FlexiBUS provides {Communication}. Devices support identification and can be attached dynamically while the bus is inactive. Before normal operation, the host reads the peripheral ROM metadata: {Peripheral ROM metadata}.

specification.chapter_name: Core transport — Published interfaces and compatibility
specification.description:
1978 baseline and later published compatibility programme. Requirements and qualification gates are not assertions of completed tests.

The technical specification is published for third-party implementation. Manufacturers can build non-exclusive, independently branded devices; adopting Logix software or video is optional. Logix commits to forward peripheral compatibility across future computer generations, using the published contracts, including {Keyboard standard reference} for keyboard behaviour.

Plotter, modem and specialist classes still need designed and qualified profiles and drivers. Discovery metadata alone does not establish that a device works.

DRI leads the software interfaces, Logix contributes hardware specifications, and independent manufacturers participate. The final governance charter, fees and support period remain open.

specification.chapter_name: Core transport — Electrical link and operating rates
specification.description:
1978 baseline and later published compatibility programme. Requirements and qualification gates are not assertions of completed tests.

Each host port connects to one device through separate differential transmit and receive pairs using asynchronous serial framing. The v1 topology does not support passive multidrop connections or implicit daisy chains.

Supported raw rates are {Supported rate (bps)} bps. A port starts at {Startup rate bps} bps. The cable target is a shielded connection up to 3 m at 500 kbit/s, subject to signal-integrity testing and qualification of period-appropriate line components.

The electrical drawing must define the power contacts, current limits and keyed connector pinout. Disk and printer devices are self-powered; keyboard power is current-limited.

Attach or detach a device only while its port is quiescent. Ground-first contacts and power sequencing must be specified; the design does not claim unrestricted live hot-plugging.

specification.chapter_name: Core transport — Message framing and flow control
specification.description:
1978 baseline and later published compatibility programme. Requirements and qualification gates are not assertions of completed tests.

Messages use 8N1 byte transport, a 0x7E delimiter, and escaping for delimiter and escape bytes. The header contains {Header}, followed by a payload of at most {Max payload bytes} bytes.

CRC-16-CCITT protects the unescaped header and payload. Its polynomial is {CRC polynomial}, its initial value is {CRC initial value}, and its final XOR value is {CRC final XOR}; reflection is disabled. The wire specification must fix byte order before implementation.

Initially, each device can have one outstanding request. Explicit ACK/NAK responses, bounded timeouts and retries, a BUSY indication and response credit provide flow control.

parameters.value: protocol version, message class, flags, request ID, payload length

specification.chapter_name: Core transport — Commands, retries and driver responsibilities
specification.description:
1978 baseline and later published compatibility programme. Requirements and qualification gates are not assertions of completed tests.

The command set includes {Commands}. Sequence and request identifiers prevent duplicate execution; the device retains its last completed request and response until the session resets. A write retry carries the same identity, and a media change invalidates queued requests.

Reset starts a new session epoch. If a non-idempotent operation such as printing has an uncertain outcome, report that uncertainty rather than silently retrying it. Removal, CRC errors, timeouts and unsupported operations are reported through stable OS errors.

Disk devices buffer complete sectors locally, so host throughput need not match the raw disk bit rate. With 8N1 framing, {Fast link rate} permits at most {Fast link ceiling}, and {Slow link rate} permits at most {Slow link ceiling}, before headers, escaping and turnaround. Keyboard polling must not monopolise the CPU during disk transfers.

Device descriptors and class protocols are architecture-neutral. The host OS supplies Z80 or ERA class drivers. Any optional device-specific ROM driver must identify its ISA and ABI explicitly; a Z80 ROM driver must never be executed as ERA code.

specification.description:
1978 baseline and later published compatibility programme. Requirements and qualification gates are not assertions of completed tests.

Qualification must exercise the host and peripheral together. Check FIFO overrun and worst-case CPU service latency, printer backpressure, disk retry after a lost reply, CRC faults, cable removal and power sequencing. These are required tests, not a statement that qualification has already passed.

specification.chapter_name: 1982 pointing-device class — Discovery and event transport
specification.description:
Optional class introduced at NCC on 7 June 1982. Existing transport framing and rates apply; this does not create FlexiBUS v2.

The pointing device uses {Transport reference} with versioned class discovery and bounded reports. Motion and button transitions must survive retry without being applied twice.

Pointing-device class, {Button count}, relative X/Y, {Roller axes}; versioned capability record. Use negotiated existing FlexiBUS rates, framing, CRC and request/response discipline.

Sequenced bounded report: accumulated signed relative X/Y motion, signed vertical/horizontal roller deltas, current button mask and ordered button transitions. ACK/retry must not duplicate motion or clicks.

Host polls with a bounded service budget; device buffers events. Coalesce motion but preserve button transitions; report overflow and resynchronize button state on reset/removal.

specification.chapter_name: 1982 pointing-device class — Controls and host compatibility
specification.description:
Optional class introduced at NCC on 7 June 1982. Existing transport framing and rates apply; this does not create FlexiBUS v2.

Buttons and independent rollers have defined actions. Host drivers preserve the common protocol across architectures and retain the bus attachment restrictions.

Button and roller reports carry input data. User-facing selection, focus and scrolling meanings belong to the 1982 pointer extension in technology.logix_tui_standard.

Architecture-neutral class driver for Z80 CP/M Platform Extensions and ERA AIONix. Attach while port quiescent; no unsupported hot-plug claim.

An expansion board carries identification and driver code in ROM so the host can configure it automatically. Boards do not require manual configuration switches. Reserved connector capacity permits later extensions without promising that every future board is already supported.

The expansion device carries its driver and identification code in ROM.

The host identifies and starts the device automatically without manual switch configuration.

Connector and pin standards may reserve unused capacity for later generations.

System and application components may execute directly from ROM where practical. Keeping suitable code and constants in ROM reduces RAM demand. Replaceable ROM/EEPROM cartridges distribute system and application software; replacing the relevant cartridge upgrades its software or firmware and provides controlled, replaceable system images.

The Aurelia June 1978 baseline, later Artemis raster profiles and June 1982 horizontal-retrace palette extension are distinct scopes. Raster sizes are capability profiles, not protocol version numbers. Monitor/controller support must be intersected; a new resolution or palette feature is not automatically present on old monitors. Hardware-specific scaling examples remain explanatory, not universal requirements. The professional 800×600 integration recorded in June 1982 is not silently added to this record’s currently specified raster tables; its exact link/timing contract requires separate review.

The link carries {Digital data width bits} data bits over a cable with {Cable}. Separate clock, control and synchronisation signals accompany the pixel data.

The cable also includes a base or reference connection.

The cable carries the following signals: {Signals}.

technology.name: Logix TUI interaction standard
technology.description: Common controls, keyboard/editing conventions and later pointer interaction, with explicit host and terminal profiles.

specification.description: The Aurelia launch on 5 June 1978 establishes the commercial keyboard/control baseline. The developer launch follows on 6 June. Keyboard conventions are core TUI requirements, not a separate ecosystem standard. External CP/M extension qualification begins on 10 November 1978 and portable extensions are released on 5 May 1979. ERA/AIONix is a later platform implementation at the Artemis launch on 19 May 1980; it does not retroactively give Aurelia multiple concurrent applications. Pointer interaction is an optional extension introduced on 7 June 1982, retaining keyboard operation. No separately released TUI 2.0 is established by these records. Software editions and qualified builds implement the standard; optional terminal profiles do not redefine native TUI shortcuts.

specification.description:
Common contract across supported hosts. Mouse references apply only from June 1982; ERA/AIONix-specific capabilities apply to the later host profile, not the 1978 Aurelia baseline.

Applications share controls and editing conventions rather than defining incompatible interfaces. A system clipboard is available. The same conventions cover the listed application classes.

Applications can use the common developer API.

The cursor moves by character.

Ctrl changes cursor movement to whole words.

Shift extends text selection.

Ctrl-C copies the selection.

Ctrl-V pastes clipboard content.

Ctrl-X cuts the selection.

The portable API is {API reference} and display services use {Display API reference}. Layout, editing, input and lifecycle services provide the same meanings across the supported hosts.

specification.chapter_name: Common interaction — Context ownership and platform compatibility
specification.description:
Common contract across supported hosts. Mouse references apply only from June 1982; ERA/AIONix-specific capabilities apply to the later host profile, not the 1978 Aurelia baseline.

Each application owns its interface state. Host differences affect resource and lifecycle capabilities, but do not silently change the meaning of the common API.

Per-application context state; no accidental shared cursor, selection or editing globals. Aurelia remains single-foreground; Artemis may manage multiple isolated application contexts.

Keep the same API behavior across Aurelia, Aurelia+ and Artemis.

Do not assume display stride, video RAM address, last column or direct peripheral registers.

Legacy CP/M console behavior is preserved; Logix-aware interfaces use the documented editing conventions.

Artemis implementation mediates process access to shared clipboard and display services.

specification.chapter_name: Common interaction — Development, implementation ownership and reuse
specification.description:
Common contract across supported hosts. Mouse references apply only from June 1982; ERA/AIONix-specific capabilities apply to the later host profile, not the 1978 Aurelia baseline.

Logix, DRI and AION jointly maintain the interface specification. AION develops the CP/M TUI and delivers source, tests and documentation to DRI. DRI owns, integrates and maintains the accepted CP/M implementation and licenses it non-exclusively. AION retains explicit rights to reuse and adapt the shared source and technology on other processors and operating systems. Pre-existing AION components remain AION-owned with perpetual CP/M maintenance and redistribution rights for DRI. The interface contract distinguishes implementation rights from ownership of applications using it.

specification.chapter_name: Keyboard and editing core — Scope and assignment rules
specification.description:
Native keyboard/editing requirements belong to the TUI core. Terminal and application-lifecycle profiles apply only where the host implements them; later operating-system terminology is design context, not a historical release claim.

Native Logix applications use a common command vocabulary. Terminal compatibility profiles remain explicit so an editing shortcut cannot silently become a process-control command.

Native Logix-aware editors, forms, spreadsheets, file views and application lifecycle. Legacy CP/M console and Unix-compatible terminal sessions retain explicitly selected compatibility profiles.

Forward-looking alternative-history design at the TUI launch; later DOS, Windows and Linux conventions are design references, not claimed historical 1978 standards.

Arrows navigate; Ctrl modifies navigation granularity; Shift extends selection using the same movement destination.

Ctrl supplies editing/document commands; Alt supplies menu and system actions. System-reserved commands cannot be rebound by applications.

Dispatch stable logical command identifiers separately from physical keys. Resolve focused control, active dialog, application and system ownership explicitly.

Show shortcuts in menus/help; disabled or unavailable commands report their state. Compatibility profiles are explicit, visible and never silently mixed.

specification.description:
Native keyboard/editing requirements belong to the TUI core. Terminal and application-lifecycle profiles apply only where the host implements them; later operating-system terminology is design context, not a historical release claim.

Navigation commands move the caret or selection by a defined unit. Shift extends the same movement; selection clearing respects active menus and dialogs. For example, character movement uses Left / Right.

Copy, cut, paste and undo have shared logical commands. Keyboard aliases retain the same command scope. Copy uses Ctrl+C; alias Ctrl+Insert, while paste uses Ctrl+V; alias Shift+Insert.

specification.description:
Native keyboard/editing requirements belong to the TUI core. Terminal and application-lifecycle profiles apply only where the host implements them; later operating-system terminology is design context, not a historical release claim.

Document commands cover creation, opening, saving, search and closure. Save uses Ctrl+S; the application must still report errors and protect modified work.

specification.chapter_name: Keyboard and editing core — Focus, dialogs and application lifecycle
specification.description:
Native keyboard/editing requirements belong to the TUI core. Terminal and application-lifecycle profiles apply only where the host implements them; later operating-system terminology is design context, not a historical release claim.

Focus and lifecycle commands are dispatched to the appropriate control, dialog, application or system. Cooperative cancellation uses Ctrl+Break; it does not imply forced termination.

specification.chapter_name: Keyboard and editing core — Editing behaviour and ownership of state
specification.description:
Native keyboard/editing requirements belong to the TUI core. Terminal and application-lifecycle profiles apply only where the host implements them; later operating-system terminology is design context, not a historical release claim.

Shared behaviour defines selection boundaries, clipboard failure handling, saving and context-sensitive keys. Resource limits and the single-foreground Aurelia model still apply.

Fixed anchor and moving caret. Plain Left/Right collapses to the corresponding selection edge without an extra step; vertical motion retains the preferred column. Home/End target displayed-line boundaries.

Shared word-boundary implementation groups letters, digits and underscore; freeze punctuation/whitespace traversal in conformance examples. Plain-text paragraphs are separated by blank lines; structured editors use paragraph objects.

Copy/Cut without a selection does nothing. Cut removes data only after clipboard transfer succeeds. Delete preserves clipboard. Typing or pasting replaces a selection as one undoable operation; allocation failure must not partially destroy selected content.

Report Save success only after successful completion; retain modified state on failure. Close offers Save/Discard/Cancel for modified content; Quit checks every modified document.

Spreadsheet navigation selects cells until cell-edit mode, which uses text rules. Editor Tab indents and Shift+Tab unindents; form Tab traverses focus. F6 leaves a multiline editor. Esc acts on only one innermost context per press.

Insertion mode by default. Overwrite is an explicit visibly indicated option; bare Insert does not toggle it by default.

Formatting Ctrl+B/I/U is optional in capable editors. Whole-line deletion, duplication, transpose and rectangular selection remain menu commands outside the common shortcut core.

Aurelia remains single-foreground. Alt+Tab exposes the supported launcher/switch mechanism and does not promise concurrent applications or preserved running state. Query lifecycle capabilities on each host.

specification.chapter_name: Keyboard and editing core — Terminal compatibility profiles
specification.description:
Native keyboard/editing requirements belong to the TUI core. Terminal and application-lifecycle profiles apply only where the host implements them; later operating-system terminology is design context, not a historical release claim.

Terminal sessions may assign control keys to interrupt, suspend or line editing. These are explicit terminal profiles, separate from the native TUI keymap. Terminal copy uses Ctrl+Shift+C.

Native TUI Ctrl+S/Q are Save/Quit and must not be intercepted by software flow control. Terminal sessions may preserve configured XON/XOFF behavior.

Optional WordStar/Emacs profiles are whole opt-in keymaps, not conflicting default aliases. Legacy CP/M control-character semantics are preserved outside native TUI contexts.

Use {SUSPEND} for suspend (if supported/configured).

specification.description:
Native keyboard/editing requirements belong to the TUI core. Terminal and application-lifecycle profiles apply only where the host implements them; later operating-system terminology is design context, not a historical release claim.

The keyboard is {Input contract keyboard reference} and transport uses {Input contract transport reference}. Events must preserve key identity and modifiers; byte-terminal fallbacks must advertise limitations instead of promising ambiguous shortcuts.

Key identity plus Ctrl/Shift/Alt modifier state; text translation is separate. Preserve Ctrl+Shift navigation and Ctrl+Shift letter distinctions.

Traditional byte terminals can conflate Tab/Ctrl+I, Enter/Ctrl+M, Esc/Ctrl+[, Backspace/Ctrl+H and shifted Ctrl letters. Advertise capabilities and offer menu equivalents rather than ambiguous shortcut promises.

Existing keyboard exact layout, event encoding, rollover and firmware remain engineering gates; required controls are conformance requirements, not a qualified new hardware revision.

Input services use {Input contract API reference}. A conforming keyboard provides {Input contract required controls}. The shared input and display contracts are documented in {Related technology references}.

specification.chapter_name: 1982 pointer extension — Standard controls and pointer interaction
specification.description:
Optional extension introduced at NCC on 7 June 1982. Older applications require the qualified service-update or relink path described here; no blanket retrofit is promised.

The mouse extension builds on {Base standard reference} and uses {Device class reference}. Standard controls receive semantic actions while retaining keyboard operation, clipping, capture and modal behaviour.

Hit-test visible enabled standard controls; primary click focuses fields/selects list items and activates buttons/menu actions.

Text widgets support click-to-place caret and drag selection; scrollbar and roller actions respect widget bounds.

Capture drags to their originating context, release on button-up/cancel/removal, respect modal dialogs and clipping.

Vertical roller scrolls the hovered scrollable control, falling back to the focused control; thumb roller similarly scrolls horizontally.

Dispatch existing semantic actions to applications; keyboard shortcuts remain fully functional.

Primary button focuses/selects/activates; secondary opens context actions where provided. Middle-finger roller scrolls vertically; thumb roller scrolls horizontally. Wheels have no implicit press buttons.

specification.chapter_name: 1982 pointer extension — Application compatibility and event ownership
specification.description:
Optional extension introduced at NCC on 7 June 1982. Older applications require the qualified service-update or relink path described here; no blanket retrofit is promised.

Existing applications gain pointer support only through compatible replaceable services or a qualified relink. Input remains owned by the active context, and a hardware cursor consumes an existing sprite resource.

No application source changes for standard controls managed by the TUI library. Existing binaries gain support only when they call replaceable/system TUI services; statically linked copies require relinking with the updated library. Custom drawing, direct console polling and non-TUI applications require explicit adaptation. No blanket mouse retrofit for all CP/M programs.

Aurelia has one foreground application; AIONix routes events only to the appropriate active/context-owned controls, with modal/capture rules and no input leakage.

Library-managed pointer with bounded save/restore on software-rendered targets or optional sprite rendering; application code need not change. A hardware pointer consumes an existing sprite unless separately provisioned; no sixth sprite is implied.

technology.name: AION C language and portable platform standard
technology.description: Shared C source-level contracts, platform services, display services and distinct target profiles; no cross-target binary compatibility is implied.

specification.description: The Z80/enhanced-CP/M developer environment launches on 6 June 1978. ERA/AIONix exploratory work begins on 1 February 1978, but its commercial developer environment belongs to the Artemis launch on 19 May 1980. These are coexisting target profiles of one source-portability contract, not successive standard versions. The platform API is explicitly labelled 1.0; this is not evidence that every module or later operating system has the same release number. Each target retains its own compiler, libraries, ABI and resource constraints. Optional graphics capabilities must be queried. Networking belongs to the 1981 programme; mouse/professional graphics integration belongs to the 1982 programme. Athena/AIONix2 compatibility is a later planning/qualification commitment, not a released capability of the original standard. A new contract revision requires a documented semantic or compatibility change; no new revision numbers are invented.

specification.chapter_name: Source portability and build profiles — Source portability and shared contracts
specification.description:
Cross-platform family overview. Z80/CP/M availability is June 1978; ERA/AIONix availability is May 1980. Later-host features do not become available on earlier computers through source portability alone.

The framework targets {Targets}. Applications share source code, libraries and API meanings; moving between instruction sets still requires a target-specific build.

Recompile shared application code with the target compiler and target libraries. Adapt OS-specific modules, resource budgets and assembly; binary compatibility is a separate CP/M-80 module path.

The framework aims to show third-party developers that moving from the 8-bit platform to Artemis is comparatively easy.

Its portability mechanisms are {Mechanisms}. Shared contracts are defined in {Shared contract references}.

technology.name: AION wafer traceability, process control and yield engineering
technology.description: Control of the Cambridge fabrication line through traceable lots, measured process windows, failure analysis and controlled recipe changes.

specification.description: Trace every wafer through incoming material, mask revision, tool, operator and recipe to its wafer map and final-test bin. Monitor particle adders, oxide thickness and integrity, sheet resistance, threshold voltage, junction leakage, contact resistance and alignment using control wafers and scribe-line structures. Separate random defects from systematic signatures; stop and contain affected lots when a control limit is exceeded.

Use split lots and designed experiments to isolate implant dose, oxidation, anneal, cleaning and contact effects. Release a change only after independent confirmation lots and reliability review. Qualify alternate tools and post-maintenance recovery with the same controls; retain golden wafers, spare critical assemblies and a frozen production route. Selected dry etches require layer-specific damage and residue qualification.

Report wafer completion as completed production wafers divided by started production wafers; accepted electrical yield as die meeting the released grade divided by gross candidate die on completed wafers; and assembly/final-test yield as accepted packaged parts divided by accepted die sent to assembly. Keep engineering wafers, rejects, downgraded bins and rework separately traceable. Good output per start is the product of gross die and these three fractions. Measure cycle-time distributions and work in process as well as output; do not confuse installed tools, forecasts or shipped volume with qualified spare capacity.

technology.name: AION memory characterisation and production testing
technology.description: Wafer-probe, packaged-device and reliability tests supporting separate ROM, SRAM and DRAM release decisions.

specification.description: Verify ROM images and address decoding against the customer-approved pattern; test SRAM reads, writes, standby current and pattern sensitivity. For DRAM, cover retention, refresh addressing, sense margins, coupling, disturb, leakage and supply sequencing. Run walking, checkerboard and March-style patterns with deliberately stressful addresses and transitions; correlate wafer and packaged tests against characterized samples. Define each timing grade at its specified voltage and temperature corners.

Qualify independent wafer lots and package lots, including alternate approved routes. Before release, specify sample sizes, acceptance limits and test conditions for powered high-temperature life, temperature cycling, humidity/package integrity and bond checks. A {life_hours}-hour powered life test uses multiple lots and documented junction temperature and electrical bias; it supports qualification, not an invented field failure rate. Contain failures, perform physical/electrical analysis and requalify the affected process or assembly change. Screening cannot substitute for correcting an unstable process.

Record probe maps, speed and retention bins, assembly traceability and final acceptance. Validate test coverage, calibration, fixture contact, test time and station availability against the committed mix; correlate independently staffed stations. Qualified outside assemblers receive controlled die maps and package drawings; AION owns incoming inspection and final release. Maintain an approved alternate assembly route and buffer stock against disruptions.

Map defects and programme redundancy only on revisions that physically implement it, followed by full retest. The initial 1 Kbit SRAM, 4 Kbit SRAM and 16 Kbit DRAM receive no assumed spare-row, laser-repair or future stepper yield benefit.
